Q: AWS Snowball vs AWS DMS A:

This is definitely a badly designed question. Official AWS exam questions will be much better quality. So, don't get too worried about individual example questions from random sources.

It would appear that the main goal is to test that you know:

  • Copying 10TB of data will take too long
  • AWS DMS can 'catch-up' on data changes from a source system

So, I'd potentially favour a C-type answer since it tests both of those knowledge components.

A. is badly worded
B. is too slow
C. shows understanding
D. is trying to trick you with Schema Conversion, which isn't required

Bottom line: Use better sources of example questions.

Q: How to use Pandas Pivot tables to make new columns combining column names and values in those columns A:

It needs

new_df = df.pivot(index="ID", columns="Day")

to get

    Data1              Data2                    Data3                 Data4
Day     1     2    3       1       2          3     1   2   3             1                      2                         3
ID
100  1035   657  995  [1, 2]     [4]  [3, 1, 2]    69  25  14  [1, 2, 2, 4]  [3, 3, 3, 2, 1, 4, 4]        [3, 2, 2, 4, 4, 2]
200   107  2539  987     [2]  [4, 2]     [3, 2]    55  80  71        [1, 4]     [4, 2, 1, 1, 1, 3]  [3, 4, 2, 1, 4, 4, 2, 3]

So rows are OK but it has multiindex headers and it needs to flatten them

new_names = [f"{col[1]}{col[0]}" for col in new_df.columns]
new_df.columns = new_names

and it gives

    1Data1  2Data1  3Data1  1Data2  2Data2     3Data2  1Data3  2Data3  3Data3        1Data4                 2Data4                    3Data4
ID
100    1035     657     995  [1, 2]     [4]  [3, 1, 2]      69      25      14  [1, 2, 2, 4]  [3, 3, 3, 2, 1, 4, 4]        [3, 2, 2, 4, 4, 2]
200     107    2539     987     [2]  [4, 2]     [3, 2]      55      80      71        [1, 4]     [4, 2, 1, 1, 1, 3]  [3, 4, 2, 1, 4, 4, 2, 3]

Now it needs to change order of columns to get expected result - first all 1Data..., next all 2Data..., etc. but it can be sorted by column names

sorted_df = new_df[sorted(new_df.columns)]

Result:

     1Data1  1Data2  1Data3        1Data4  2Data1  2Data2  2Data3                 2Data4  3Data1     3Data2  3Data3                    3Data4
ID
100    1035  [1, 2]      69  [1, 2, 2, 4]     657     [4]      25  [3, 3, 3, 2, 1, 4, 4]     995  [3, 1, 2]      14        [3, 2, 2, 4, 4, 2]
200     107     [2]      55        [1, 4]    2539  [4, 2]      80     [4, 2, 1, 1, 1, 3]     987     [3, 2]      71  [3, 4, 2, 1, 4, 4, 2, 3]

And finally it may need to convert index ID back to column

final_df = sorted_df.reset_index()

Final result:

    ID  1Data1  1Data2  1Data3        1Data4  2Data1  2Data2  2Data3                 2Data4  3Data1     3Data2  3Data3                    3Data4
0  100    1035  [1, 2]      69  [1, 2, 2, 4]     657     [4]      25  [3, 3, 3, 2, 1, 4, 4]     995  [3, 1, 2]      14        [3, 2, 2, 4, 4, 2]
1  200     107     [2]      55        [1, 4]    2539  [4, 2]      80     [4, 2, 1, 1, 1, 3]     987     [3, 2]      71  [3, 4, 2, 1, 4, 4, 2, 3]

Full working code:

import pandas as pd

ID = [100, 100, 100, 200, 200, 200]
Day = [1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3]
Data1 = [1035, 657, 995, 107, 2539, 987]
Data2 = [[1, 2], [4], [3, 1, 2], [2], [4, 2], [3, 2]]
Data3 = [69, 25, 14, 55, 80, 71]
Data4 = [
    [1, 2, 2, 4],
    [3, 3, 3, 2, 1, 4, 4],
    [3, 2, 2, 4, 4, 2],
    [1, 4],
    [4, 2, 1, 1, 1, 3],
    [3, 4, 2, 1, 4, 4, 2, 3],
]

df = pd.DataFrame(
    data={
        "ID": ID,
        "Day": Day,
        "Data1": Data1,
        "Data2": Data2,
        "Data3": Data3,
        "Data4": Data4,
    }
)

print(df)

new_df = df.pivot(index="ID", columns="Day")
print(new_df)
print(new_df.columns)

new_names = [f"{col[1]}{col[0]}" for col in new_df.columns]
new_df.columns = new_names
print(new_df)

sorted_df = new_df[sorted(new_df.columns)]
print(sorted_df)

final_df = sorted_df.reset_index()
print(final_df)

Q: How to demonstrate Data Engineering capabilities? A:

There's nothing here to review yet: This is a list of services, not a project. Anyone can write this description in a few minutes; an LLM can write it in seconds. It shows nothing about what you actually built or understand.

Put the code on GitHub. Then the questions worth asking answer themselves: why Kinesis, not Kafka, in the cloud version? What partitioning did you choose in S3 and why? What breaks when the schema changes, and how does Iceberg handle it in your code? What does a bad/duplicate/late record do to your pipeline? How much does a day of this cost?

A reviewer can't tell a working pipeline from a paragraph. The description is worth nothing — the repo, the tradeoffs you made, and the problems you hit are the entire thing. Publish that, and you'll get real feedback.

Q: LangChain "ChatOpenAI" LLM exceeding token length when using RetrievalQA to answer multiple questions A:

The issue is most likely not chat history. Each new ChatOpenAI instance starts fresh so creating it inside the loop does not cause previous questions to accumulate.

The problem is that your entire document is being passed as context to the model. In your code you create the vector store with:

embeddings = Chroma.from_texts([document_text], embedding_client)

Since the whole document is stored as a single chunk RetrievalQA can retrieve that entire document for every question. If the document is large enough the prompt sent to the model can exceed the model's context window.

You should split the document into smaller chunks before creating the embeddings. For example:

from langchain.text_splitter import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter

text_splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(
    chunk_size=2000,
    chunk_overlap=200
)

documents = text_splitter.create_documents([document_text])

embeddings = Chroma.from_documents(
    documents,
    embedding_client
)

llm = ChatOpenAI(
    model="gpt-3.5-turbo",
    temperature=0,
    max_tokens=1000
)

retriever = RetrievalQA.from_chain_type(
    llm,
    retriever=embeddings.as_retriever(
        search_kwargs={"k": 4}
    )
)

answer = retriever.invoke({"query": question})

Now the retriever will return only the most relevant chunks instead of sending the entire document to the model.

Also max_tokens controls how much the model can generate it does not reduce the size of the input context. The important part here is reducing the amount of document text being retrieved and sent to the model.

So you do not need to recreate ChatOpenAI for every question. The main fix is to chunk the document and limit how many chunks RetrievalQA retrieves.

Q: Prevent AI tooling from making changes to the DB A:

We have a separate database team than the development team I work on. We can task them to create a readonly user for the AI, but we'd rather not go through that trouble, if possible.

Why not? This problem has nothing to do with AI - you just have some process which you think should be able to read from the database but should not be able to write to it. And that's exactly what database privileges are there for.

For any non-trivial system, this should be a routine thing to do. E.g. if you have some process which does reporting, it should have its own service account (for auditing), and since a report typically doesn't need write access, it shouldn't be given write access.

Q: Convert typedef struct from C++ to Python A:

Python doesn't have structs, but it does have dataclasses which are functionally the same:

(I cant make codeblocks, or indent, without stack overflow crashing. Can someone edit this into a codeblock with indents?)

"""

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass

class Word:

<indent>word: str

"""

Your error:

" TypeError: _init_() missing 1 required positional argument: 'n' "

Is occurring because you needed to initialize Word with a value.

Also, you don't really need to use a typedef in python for this, since you can just use the class name, but there is a python equivalent for typedef:

"""

# the same as 'typedef vector<Word> Words;'

type Words = list[Word]

"""

Q: Error in `check_aesthetics using ggplot in R A:

It appears you omitted aes() in the second geom_line. A better approach is to stack the data frame in long format and use the col name as aesthetic.

library(tidyr)

ggplot(pivot_longer(PhyChl, c(phyc, chl)), aes(x=time, y=value, color=name ))+
  geom_line()
